claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known mechanism of translational control during hypoxia.

claims.claim: Most (lymph)angiogenic genes are induced at the translatome level in hypoxic HL-1 mouse cardiomyocytes.
claims.source: Here, we report the transcriptome and translatome signatures of (lymph)angiogenic genes in hypoxic HL-1 mouse cardiomyocytes: most genes are induced at the translatome level, including all IRES-containing mRNAs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the polysome profiling data presented in Figure 2C showing 94% of genes with increased polysome recruitment.

claims.claim: All IRES-containing mRNAs are induced at the translatome level in hypoxic HL-1 mouse cardiomyocytes.
claims.source: Here, we report the transcriptome and translatome signatures of (lymph)angiogenic genes in hypoxic HL-1 mouse cardiomyocytes: most genes are induced at the translatome level, including all IRES-containing mRNAs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 3B showing increased polysome recruitment for all detectable IRES-containing mRNAs.

claims.claim: (Lymph)angiogenic factor mRNA IRESs are activated in early hypoxia.
claims.source: Our data reveal activation of (lymph)angiogenic factor mRNA IRESs in early hypoxia.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the bicistronic reporter assay data in Figure 4D showing IRES activation at 4 and 8 hours of hypoxia.

claims.claim: Vasohibin1 (VASH1) is an IRES trans-acting factor (ITAF).
claims.source: We identify vasohibin1 (VASH1) as an IRES trans-acting factor (ITAF) that is able to bind RNA and to activate the FGF1 IRES in hypoxia, but which tends to inhibit several IRESs in normoxia.
claims.evidence: This is supported by BIA-MS data showing VASH1 binding to IRESs (Figure 5), SPR data showing RNA binding (Figure 5D-F), and functional data showing IRES regulation (Figure 7).

claims.claim: VASH1 is able to bind RNA.
claims.source: We identify vasohibin1 (VASH1) as an IRES trans-acting factor (ITAF) that is able to bind RNA and to activate the FGF1 IRES in hypoxia, but which tends to inhibit several IRESs in normoxia.
claims.evidence: This is supported by surface plasmon resonance data showing direct RNA binding with affinity constants of 6.5-9.6 nM (Figure 5D-F).

claims.claim: VASH1 activates the FGF1 IRES in hypoxia.
claims.source: We identify vasohibin1 (VASH1) as an IRES trans-acting factor (ITAF) that is able to bind RNA and to activate the FGF1 IRES in hypoxia, but which tends to inhibit several IRESs in normoxia.
claims.evidence: This is supported by knockdown experiments showing 64% decrease in FGF1 IRES activity upon VASH1 depletion in hypoxia (Figure 7D).

claims.claim: VASH1 tends to inhibit several IRESs in normoxia.
claims.source: We identify vasohibin1 (VASH1) as an IRES trans-acting factor (ITAF) that is able to bind RNA and to activate the FGF1 IRES in hypoxia, but which tends to inhibit several IRESs in normoxia.
claims.evidence: This is supported by knockdown data showing moderate increases in IRES activities (13-16%) in normoxia, significant for VEGFD and EMCV IRESs (Figure 7C).

claims.claim: VASH1 depletion has a wide impact on the translatome of (lymph)angiogenesis genes.
claims.source: VASH1 depletion has a wide impact on the translatome of (lymph)angiogenesis genes, suggesting that this protein can regulate translation positively or negatively in early hypoxia.
claims.evidence: This is supported by polysome profiling data showing that VASH1 depletion affects 60-70% of mRNAs in both normoxia and hypoxia (Figure 8).

claims.claim: VASH1 can regulate translation positively or negatively in early hypoxia.
claims.source: VASH1 depletion has a wide impact on the translatome of (lymph)angiogenesis genes, suggesting that this protein can regulate translation positively or negatively in early hypoxia.
claims.evidence: This is supported by polysome profiling showing both activation (22-44%) and inhibition (29-41%) of mRNA recruitment upon VASH1 depletion (Figure 8).

claims.claim: Translational control is a pivotal process triggering new vessel formation in ischemic heart.
claims.source: Translational control thus appears as a pivotal process triggering new vessel formation in ischemic heart.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive data showing predominant translational regulation of angiogenic genes in cardiomyocytes.

claims.claim: Lymphangiogenesis is induced by hypoxia.
claims.source: Recently it has been shown that lymphangiogenesis is also induced by hypoxia (Morfoisse et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Hypoxia-induced (lymph)angiogenesis is mediated by strong modification of gene expression at both transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels.
claims.source: Hypoxia-induced (lymph)angiogenesis is mediated by strong modification of gene expression at both transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels (Pouysségur et al., 2006; Holcik and Sonenberg, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: HIF1 is a transcription factor stabilized by oxygen deprivation that activates transcription from promoters containing hypoxia-responsive elements (HRE).
claims.source: A major mode of regulation of gene expression is mediated at the transcriptional level by the hypoxia inducible factor 1 (HIF1), a transcription factor stabilized by oxygen deprivation, that activates transcription from promoters containing hypoxia-responsive elements (HRE).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about HIF1 function.

claims.claim: VEGFA is a major angiogenic factor and a well-described HIF1 target.
claims.source: One of the well-described HIF1 targets is vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA), a major angiogenic factor (Forsythe et al., 1996; Pagès and Pouysségur, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: FGF2 is induced by hypoxia in a HIF-independent manner by a translational mechanism.
claims.source: However, two other major angiogenic or lymphangiogenic growth factors, fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2) and VEGFC, respectively, are induced by hypoxia in a HIF-independent manner by a translational mechanism, indicating the importance of the post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression in this process (Morfoisse et al., 2014; Conte et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: VEGFC is induced by hypoxia in a HIF-independent manner by a translational mechanism.
claims.source: However, two other major angiogenic or lymphangiogenic growth factors, fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2) and VEGFC, respectively, are induced by hypoxia in a HIF-independent manner by a translational mechanism, indicating the importance of the post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression in this process (Morfoisse et al., 2014; Conte et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Translation of mRNAs by the classical cap-dependent mechanism is silenced during stress.
claims.source: In particular, translation of mRNAs by the classical cap-dependent mechanism is silenced, whereas alternative translation mechanisms allow enhanced expression of a small group of messengers that are involved in the control of cell survival (Holcik and Sonenberg, 2005; Baird et al., 2006; Spriggs et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: IRESs correspond to RNA structural elements that allow the direct recruitment of the ribosome onto mRNA.
claims.source: One of the major alternative mechanisms that is able to overcome this global inhibition of translation by stress depends on internal ribosome entry sites (IRESs), which correspond to RNA structural elements that allow the direct recruitment of the ribosome onto mRNA.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about IRES function.

claims.claim: RNA-binding proteins called IRES trans-acting factors (ITAFs) are able to stabilize the adequate RNA conformation, thus allowing ribosome recruitment.
claims.source: As regards the molecular mechanisms of IRES activation by stress, several studies have reported that RNA-binding proteins, called IRES trans-acting factors (ITAFs), are able to stabilize the adequate RNA conformation, thus allowing ribosome recruitment (Faye and Holcik, 1849; Godet et al., 2019; Liberman et al., 2015; Mitchell et al., 2003; Morfoisse et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Subcellular relocalization of ITAFs plays a critical role in IRES-dependent translation.
claims.source: Interestingly, subcellular relocalization of ITAFs plays a critical role in IRES-dependent translation (Lewis and Holcik, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Cytoplasmic relocalization of ITAFs such as PTB, PCBP1, RBM4 or nucleolin is critical to activate IRES-dependent translation.
claims.source: Indeed, many RNA-binding proteins are known to shuttle between nucleus and cytoplasm, and it has been reported that cytoplasmic relocalization of ITAFs such as PTB, PCBP1, RBM4 or nucleolin is critical to activate IRES-dependent translation (Godet et al., 2019; Morfoisse et al., 2016; Lewis and Holcik, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: hnRNPA1 may have a negative impact on IRES activity when accumulating in the cytoplasm.
claims.source: By contrast, other ITAFs such as hnRNPA1, may have a negative impact on IRES activity when accumulating in the cytoplasm (Lewis et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: IRESs are present in the mRNAs of several (lymph)angiogenic growth factors in the FGF and VEGF families.
claims.source: IRESs are present in the mRNAs of several (lymph)angiogenic growth factors in the FGF and VEGF families, suggesting that the IRES-dependent mechanism might be a major way to activate angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis during stress (Morfoisse et al., 2014; Godet et al., 2019; Morfoisse et al., 2016; Huez et al., 1998; Martineau et al., 2004; Stein et al., 1998; Vagner et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Tumoral angiogenesis leads to the formation of abnormal vessels that are non-functional, differing strongly from non-tumoral angiogenesis that induces formation of functional vessels.
claims.source: However, most studies of the role of hypoxia in the regulation of gene expression have been performed in tumoral hypoxia, although it has been reported that tumoral angiogenesis leads to the formation of abnormal vessels that are non-functional, differing strongly from non-tumoral angiogenesis that induces formation of functional vessels (Jain, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: HL-1 cells keep the beating phenotype specific to cardiomyocytes although immortalized.
claims.source: In order to analyze the expression of angiogenic and lymphangiogenic growth factors in hypoxic cardiomyocytes, the HL-1 cell line was chosen: although immortalized, it keeps the beating phenotype specific to cardiomyocyte (Claycomb et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work describing the HL-1 cell line.

results.result: In hypoxic HL-1 cardiomyocytes, transcriptional changes are limited, with only a few genes (Vegfa, PAI-1, Apelin) showing significant induction as HIF1 targets, while major angiogenic factors like FGF2 and VEGFC are transcriptionally repressed. The authors conclude that transcriptional response is not the major mechanism controlling (lymph)angiogenic factor expression, suggesting post-transcriptional mechanisms are involved.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C34 provide consistent transcriptome data from Figure 1 showing limited transcriptional induction (56% of genes induced >1.5-fold at 8h, but few strongly induced) and repression of key factors. Claims C35-C36 draw appropriate inferences from this data. The conclusion is well-supported by the experimental evidence and statistical analysis.

results.result: Translational activity decreases in hypoxic HL-1 cells (polysome/monosome ratio shifts from 1.55 to 1.40), confirmed by eIF2α phosphorylation, yet 94% of (lymph)angiogenic genes show increased polysome recruitment. The authors conclude that the main response to early hypoxia in cardiomyocytes is translational, not transcriptional.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C44 are supported by polysome profiling data (Figure 2) showing paradoxical increase in specific mRNA recruitment despite global translation inhibition. The inference in C45 is justified by comparing transcriptome (Figure 1) with translatome (Figure 2C) data. The 4E-BP1 data (C39-C40) provides additional mechanistic context.

results.result: All detectable IRES-containing angiogenic factor mRNAs (Fgf1, Vegfa, Vegfd, Cyr61, Hif1a, Igf1r) show 2-3 fold increased polysome recruitment in hypoxia as early as 4 hours, while Vegfa is the only one significantly induced at the transcriptome level. This indicates IRES-dependent translation is activated early in the hypoxic response.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C53 are supported by Figure 3A-B showing differential regulation at transcriptome vs translatome levels. The conclusion (C54-C55) that IRES-dependent translation is an early event is justified by the 4h timepoint data. However, FGF2 and VEGFC mRNAs were not detectable in polysomes, which limits the comprehensiveness of the claim about 'all' IRES-containing mRNAs.

results.result: Bicistronic reporter assays reveal two groups of IRESs with distinct temporal activation: (lymph)angiogenic factor IRESs (FGF1, FGF2, VEGFAb, VEGFC, VEGFD) are activated in early hypoxia (4-8h), while non-angiogenic IRESs (c-myc, EMCV) are activated only in late hypoxia (24h). FGF1 IRES activation correlates with increased FGF1 protein expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C61 are supported by bicistronic reporter data in Figure 4B-D showing differential temporal activation patterns. The correlation with FGF1 protein (C58) is shown in Figure 4C. The grouping inference (C62) is logical based on the temporal patterns. The use of lentivectors to overcome transfection limitations is methodologically sound.

results.result: VASH1 is identified as a novel IRES trans-acting factor with RNA-binding activity. BIA-MS shows VASH1 binds FGF1 IRES in hypoxia (4-8h) and EMCV IRES in both conditions, but not VEGFA IRES. In silico analysis predicts two RNA-binding domains, and SPR confirms direct binding to FGF1, VEGFAa, and EMCV IRESs with nanomolar affinity (6.5-9.6 nM).
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7 and C63-C71 are well-supported by multiple complementary approaches: BIA-MS (Figure 5A-C, Supplementary file 4), in silico prediction (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and SPR validation (Figure 5D-F). The nanomolar affinity constants demonstrate significant RNA-binding activity. The novelty claim (C63) is appropriately stated. However, there's an apparent inconsistency: BIA-MS shows no VEGFA binding (C66), yet SPR shows binding with 8.0 nM affinity (C69).

results.result: VASH1 is expressed in HL-1 cardiomyocytes (previously only described in endothelial cells) and is translationally induced in early hypoxia. Despite decreased mRNA levels at 4h, Vash1 mRNA shows 7-fold increased polysome recruitment, leading to increased VASH1 protein expression. VASH1 localizes to both nucleus and cytoplasm as foci that increase in size during hypoxia.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C80 are supported by multiple data types: RT-qPCR (Figure 6A), polysome profiling (Figure 6B), capillary Western (Figure 6C), and immunocytochemistry (Figure 6D-F). The translational induction inference (C77) is justified by the discordance between mRNA decrease and polysome recruitment increase. The foci size quantification (C80) is statistically significant (Figure 6F).

results.result: VASH1 knockdown (73% mRNA, 59% protein) specifically decreases FGF1 IRES activity by 64% in hypoxia, demonstrating VASH1 activates FGF1 IRES. In normoxia, VASH1 knockdown moderately increases several IRES activities (13-16%, significant for VEGFD and EMCV), suggesting VASH1 inhibits these IRESs under normoxic conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C86 are supported by knockdown data (Figure 7A-B) and bicistronic reporter assays (Figure 7C-D). The moderate protein knockdown (C82-C83) is explained by VASH1's long half-life (>24h, Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The functional specificity for FGF1 IRES in hypoxia (C85) is clear, though the moderate knockdown efficiency may underestimate the full effect. The dual role inference (C87) is supported by the opposing effects in normoxia vs hypoxia.

results.result: VASH1 depletion has broad effects on the translatome, affecting 60-70% of (lymph)angiogenic mRNAs in both normoxia and hypoxia. In normoxia, 22% of mRNAs show increased and 41% show decreased polysome recruitment; in hypoxia, 44% increase and 29% decrease. This demonstrates VASH1 can regulate translation both positively and negatively.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C93 are supported by polysome profiling data in Figure 8 showing widespread effects of VASH1 depletion. The dual role conclusion (C93) is justified by the bidirectional effects. However, the authors appropriately note (C92) that the mechanism (direct vs indirect) cannot be determined from this approach. The broad impact suggests VASH1 may have functions beyond direct IRES binding.

results.result: The authors conclude that translational control is a pivotal process triggering new vessel formation in ischemic heart, based on the predominant translational (rather than transcriptional) regulation of (lymph)angiogenic genes and IRES activation in hypoxic cardiomyocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 summarize the main findings supported by the comprehensive data. The overarching conclusion (C12) is justified by the convergent evidence from transcriptome, translatome, and IRES activity analyses. However, this conclusion is based on an in vitro cell line model (HL-1), and in vivo validation would strengthen the claim about ischemic heart.

results.result: The authors argue that moderate IRES activation (1.3-1.7 fold in their study) is physiologically significant, citing prior work showing 2-3 fold changes in VEGFC, VEGFD, and FGF1 IRES activity have substantial effects on vessel formation and differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C100 are supported by appropriate citations to prior work. This contextualizes the moderate fold-changes observed in the current study and addresses a potential criticism. The comparison to viral IRESs (C97-C100) provides additional context for interpreting cellular IRES activation levels.

results.result: HL-1 cardiomyocytes respond to hypoxia earlier (4-8h) than tumor cell lines (24h), with early activation of angiogenic IRESs. The authors speculate this may reflect cell-type-specific ITAFs and differences between non-tumoral and tumoral hypoxia responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 are supported by citations comparing HL-1 timing to tumor cell lines. However, the speculation (C105-C106) about tumor cell resistance and cell-type specificity is not directly tested. Alternative explanations (e.g., differences in culture conditions, oxygen sensing mechanisms) are not excluded. This remains a hypothesis requiring further investigation.

results.result: Despite similar binding affinities to multiple IRESs (6.5-9.6 nM), VASH1 specifically regulates FGF1 IRES in hypoxia. The authors hypothesize that IRES specificity depends not on RNA-binding specificity but on IRESome multi-partner composition, consistent with the dual role observed for other ITAFs.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C126 are supported by the functional data (Figure 7D) and SPR data (Figure 5D-F). The hypothesis (C127, C129) is reasonable and supported by citation (C128), but is not directly tested. The mechanism by which VASH1 achieves functional specificity despite promiscuous binding remains unclear and requires identification of partner proteins.

results.result: The introduction establishes background knowledge about hypoxia-induced (lymph)angiogenesis, HIF1-mediated transcriptional control, IRES-dependent translation during stress, and the role of ITAFs in IRES activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C26 are appropriately cited background knowledge establishing the context for the study. These are well-established facts in the field supported by appropriate citations. This provides the necessary foundation for understanding the significance of the current work.

results.result: HL-1 cells are an immortalized cardiomyocyte cell line that maintains the beating phenotype characteristic of cardiomyocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C27 and C101 are supported by citation to the original description of HL-1 cells (Claycomb et al., 1998). The beating phenotype is used as an authentication method, which is appropriate for this cell type.

results.result: The discussion contextualizes VASH1 findings within prior knowledge of VASH1 function in angiogenesis, stress response, and cell survival, and discusses potential mechanisms of VASH1 regulation and localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C123 appropriately cite and discuss prior work on VASH1 and other ITAFs. The speculation about VASH1 regulation by HuR (C113-C116) and stress granule localization (C122) is reasonable but not directly tested. The discussion of VASH1 isoforms (C117-C119) provides context for interpreting the results.
